reasoning: Reels drive almost all reach so far. The best performers were body and brain explainers with a 'what happens / what it really does' hook: sleep deprivation (104 reach, 2 shares), memories (94) and fear (53). Recent posts are heavy on body reflexes, so I'm moving to an everyday-science angle with the same proven hook shape. Caffeine is universal and relatable, which should help shares ('send this to your coffee friend'). It is a 5-slide reel with the direct-claim hook (version B of the hook test). Lofi music went with the top reel. Palette 0 continues the rotation. I'm not using a trial reel because with 0 followers it adds no protection.
topic: Caffeine: adenosine blocking, half-life, sleep loss, crash, withdrawal
hook: What coffee really does to your brain

slides.title: It hijacks sleep signals
slides.body: Caffeine looks like adenosine, the molecule that makes you sleepy, and blocks its receptors in your brain.
slides.image_prompt: A steaming coffee cup beside a glowing model of a brain on a dark wooden table, moody cinematic light

slides.title: Half stays for hours
slides.body: On average, half the caffeine from your cup is still in your blood about 5 hours later.
slides.image_prompt: An hourglass filled with dark coffee grounds next to an espresso cup, dramatic side lighting

slides.title: It steals your sleep
slides.body: In one study, a strong dose taken 6 hours before bed still cut total sleep by more than an hour.
slides.image_prompt: An empty coffee mug on a bedside table next to an analog alarm clock at night, blue moonlight through a window

slides.title: Why the crash hits
slides.body: Adenosine keeps piling up while it's blocked. When caffeine fades, it floods the receptors at once.
slides.image_prompt: A tipped-over empty coffee cup with a few spilled beans on a desk, dim late-afternoon light

slides.title: Your brain adapts
slides.body: Daily drinkers may grow extra adenosine receptors. Skip a day and withdrawal headaches can start within 12 to 24 hours.
slides.image_prompt: A pile of roasted coffee beans with a cracked glass cup in front, dark moody studio light

cta: Follow for facts your brain will love
caption:
Your morning coffee doesn't give you energy. It blocks the signal that tells your brain you're tired. Caffeine fits into the same receptors as adenosine, the molecule that builds sleep pressure all day.

That's why the effect lasts so long. On average, half your caffeine is still in your blood around 5 hours after your cup. A late coffee can quietly cut your sleep even if you fall asleep fine.

How many cups do you drink a day? Be honest 👇
